title: Possible Prophecies About Muhammad
subtitle: Islamic Claims of Prophecies in the Torah and Gospel, and Christian Scholarly Responses
summary: The Quran states that earlier revelation announced Muhammad, and Muslims have long connected this claim with Deuteronomy 18 and the Gospel promises of a coming advocate. The 'prophet like Moses' offers a meaningful Islamic comparison; the Paraclete argument is more disputed because John's Greek text identifies the Paraclete as the Holy Spirit. These passages can support a cumulative case, but they should not be presented as uncontested proof. The central evidence remains the Quran, Muhammad's character, and the return to pure monotheism.

sections.title: The Claim in Brief
sections.body: The Quran says earlier revelation announced Muhammad. Muslims often discuss Deuteronomy 18 and Jesus’ promise of the Paraclete. Deuteronomy offers a strong comparison with Muhammad. The Paraclete argument is more disputed. These passages support a cumulative case, not an uncontested proof.

sections.title: Two Frequently Discussed Passages
sections.body: Quran 7:157 and 61:6 guide the Muslim reading. Two passages receive special attention. Deuteronomy 18 speaks of a prophet like Moses. John 14–16 speaks of the Paraclete. The first creates a substantial comparison. The second faces a direct textual objection.

sections.title: A Prophet Like Moses
sections.body:
Deuteronomy 18:18 promises a prophet like Moses from among Israel’s “brothers.” Muslims note that Ishmaelites are related to Israelites. Muhammad and Moses both brought law. Both led communities. Both migrated under persecution. Both governed and completed a public mission. Quran 7:157 says the Messenger is described in the Torah and Gospel.

Jewish and Christian readers usually see Israel’s prophetic line. Christians also apply the passage to Jesus through Acts 3. The wording does not name Muhammad. The Islamic reading is reasoned, not an uncontested translation.

sections.title: The Paraclete and the Promise of Ahmad
sections.body:
Quran 61:6 says Jesus announced a messenger named Ahmad. Muslims connect this with the Paraclete in John. Teaching, testimony, and guidance can resemble a prophetic mission.

The difficulty must be admitted. The surviving Greek text reads parakletos, “advocate” or “helper.” John 14:26 calls the Paraclete the Holy Spirit. No known Greek manuscript reads periklytos or Ahmad. The connection may express the Quran’s claim about Jesus’ original announcement. The proposed Greek word change is not manuscript evidence.

sections.title: The Main Christian Reading
sections.body:
Christian interpreters read Deuteronomy within Israel. Acts 3 applies the passage to Jesus. They read John’s Paraclete as the Holy Spirit. John 14:26 identifies it in those words. Acts 2 describes the Spirit at Pentecost. These are strong contextual arguments.

The Muslim response is not to invent a missing manuscript. It asks whether Muhammad fits the Mosaic pattern. It also asks whether Jesus’ original announcement is fully preserved in the later Gospel form. The Quran’s independent claim belongs in the larger case for revelation.

sections.title: What the Languages Allow
sections.body:
The Hebrew word for “brothers” can mean fellow Israelites. In some settings it can mean related peoples. Context favors Israel’s institution. The wider family of Abraham still allows a Muslim comparison.

In Greek, parakletos is well attested as advocate or helper. The claim that the word was originally periklytos has no manuscript support. A careful presentation should retire that claim. It should focus on the parallels that can be defended.

sections.title: A Cumulative Argument
sections.body: Muslims discussed these passages in conversation with Jewish and Christian scripture. That history does not decide whether the reading is true. It does show the need to separate the Quran’s claim from later attempts to identify a surviving verse. These passages are supporting signs. The primary case is Muhammad’s message, the Quran, his character, and the results of his mission.

sections.title: Scriptural Basis for the Islamic Perspective
sections.body:
Quran 7:157 says believers find the Messenger described in the Torah and Gospel. Quran 61:6 presents Jesus announcing Ahmad. These verses establish the Islamic reason for examining earlier scripture. Muslim scholars therefore read Deuteronomy 18 and the Paraclete passages through the Quran’s claim that Muhammad was foretold.

This method is an Islamic interpretation. It does not erase Christian readings. It argues for continuity in divine revelation and for Muhammad as the final messenger.

sections.title: Christian Scriptural Context and Early Church Testimony
sections.body:
Christian interpretation rests on the New Testament’s wider story. Acts 3:22–26 quotes Deuteronomy and applies it to Jesus. John 14:26 calls the Paraclete “the Holy Spirit.” Acts 2 presents Pentecost as the promise’s fulfillment. Early Christian testimony supports this reading.

Muslims can acknowledge this evidence and still ask whether the Quran corrects a later interpretation. The two traditions begin with different views of revelation and Jesus.

sections.title: Why This Matters: Possible Prophecies About Muhammad
sections.body: Deuteronomy 18 is a serious part of the Muslim case. Muhammad resembles Moses as prophet, lawgiver, and community leader. The Paraclete claim is weaker as a stand-alone argument and remains disputed. The strongest case is cumulative. It includes pure monotheism, the Quran, Muhammad’s character, and the change his mission produced.

quranVerses.translation: Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil and relieves them of their burden and the shackles which were upon them. So they who have believed in him, honored him, supported him and followed the light which was sent down with him - it is those who will be the successful.

quranVerses.translation: And [mention] when Jesus, the son of Mary, said, "O children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you confirming what came before me of the Torah and bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, "This is obvious magic."

This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again Yahweh my God’s voice, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their brothers, like you. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I shall command him. It shall happen, that whoever will not listen to my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.
But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.

Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.

faq.question: Why do Muslims connect Deuteronomy 18 with Muhammad?
faq.answer: Muslims point to the promised prophet's likeness to Moses and to the word 'brothers.' Muhammad resembles Moses as a law-bearing prophet, community leader, migrant, and statesman. Jewish and Christian readers usually understand the passage within Israel, so the identification remains argued rather than explicit by name.

faq.question: Does the Greek word Paraclete mean Ahmad?
faq.answer: No known Greek manuscript reads Ahmad or periklytos. The manuscripts read parakletos, advocate or helper, and John 14:26 identifies the figure as the Holy Spirit. Muslims may still connect the promise thematically with Quran 61:6, but a claimed Greek word substitution is not supported by textual evidence.

faq.question: Does acknowledging that difficulty weaken belief in Quran 61:6?
faq.answer: It limits one proposed identification of Jesus' announcement; it does not decide whether Jesus originally foretold Muhammad or whether the Quran is revelation. Those questions must be assessed through the broader case for the Quran and Muhammad.

faq.question: What is the strongest way to use biblical prophecy in Dawah?
faq.answer: Present Deuteronomy's Mosaic comparison as supporting evidence, state Christian and Jewish readings accurately, and avoid claims that depend on a nonexistent manuscript variant. Then return to the primary evidence: the Quran's message and transmission and Muhammad's prophetic mission.
